sermon:
## The Word of Life and the Light We Walk In
*Fellowship begins where pretending ends*

**Text:** 1 John 1:1-2:2 · **Supporting:** John 1:14 · Psalm 32:3-5 · Isaiah 59:2 · Hebrews 9:14

A church had split. Teachers who once stood in the same room, broke the same bread, said the same creed, had walked out, and they walked out claiming they had gone deeper, seen more, ascended past the simple gospel into a knowledge the rest were too earthbound to reach. The people who stayed were not sure anymore. If those who left were the spiritual ones, what did that make those who remained? John writes to people whose assurance has been picked up and shaken like a jar, and he does not begin with comfort. He begins with his hands.

**What the Apostles Touched**

Read how the letter opens, and notice that John refuses to begin in the abstract. "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life" (1 John 1:1). Four verbs, and three of them are about the body. Heard. Seen. Handled. The teachers who left had a religion of escape, spirit ascending, flesh discarded, the material world a prison to be transcended. John answers them with calluses. The eternal life he preaches did not float above history. It had a face the apostles looked at and a hand they could grip.

This is the same man who wrote, "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). The Word did not visit flesh. The Word became it. And the whole weight of John's letter hangs on that refusal to let God stay safely immaterial, because a God who became touchable is a God who can be lied to with your actual life, not just your ideas. "That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you, that ye also may have fellowship with us: and truly our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ" (1 John 1:3). Fellowship. Not information. The point of the gospel John handled with his hands is that you would be brought into the life of the Father and the Son.

Not a higher knowledge. A shared life.

**The Light That Will Not Negotiate**

Then comes the message, and it is not soft. "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" (1 John 1:5). Here is where most of us start managing. We hear that God is light and we begin arranging the furniture of our souls so the lit rooms face the door and the locked ones stay in back. We call this discretion. John calls it a lie. "If we say that we have fellowship with him, and walk in darkness, we lie, and do not the truth" (1 John 1:6).

Notice what walking in the light is not. It is not sinlessness, he will say in two verses that anyone claiming sinlessness is self-deceived. Walking in the light is walking where the light reaches you, refusing the dark corner, living without the locked room. It is the willingness to be seen. David knew the alternative. "When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long" (Psalm 32:3). That is the body of a man walking in darkness, not a scandalous man, a silent one. A man whose secret was eating him from the inside while his public life looked fine. Isaiah named the cost of it plainly: "your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you" (Isaiah 59:2). Sin does not merely stain. It hides. It puts a wall where there was a face.

I know the architecture of the locked room because I have built it. I have stood in a pulpit and preached light while keeping a corner of my own house dark, and I have called the keeping of it humility, when it was only fear. The lie John names is not the lie of the scandalous. It is the lie of the respectable. We say we have no sin, and the truth is not in us, and the room with the lights off keeps growing.

**The Advocate Who Is Also the Sacrifice**

So what does John offer the man with the locked room? Not lower standards. He raises them, God is light, no darkness at all, and then he opens a door under the standard. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). Faithful and just. Not faithful and merciful, as if mercy bent justice. Just. Because the debt was paid.

"My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous: and he is the propitiation for our sins" (1 John 2:1-2). Hold those two words together. Advocate and propitiation. The advocate is the one who stands beside you before the Father and speaks for your case. The propitiation is the one who bore the wrath your case deserved. And here they are the same person. Your defense attorney is also the one who served your sentence. The blood the writer of Hebrews describes, Christ who "through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God", does what no locked room can do: it cleanses the conscience itself (Hebrews 9:14).

This is why confession in John leads not to despair but to cleansing. The man who walks in the light is not the man with nothing to confess. He is the man who no longer needs the dark, because the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses him from all sin, and the one he confesses to is the one already pleading his case.

The locked room was never protecting you. It was only keeping you from the cleansing.

Walk in the light. Confess.

## The Old Commandment Made New, and a Love That Cannot Hold the World
*You cannot love two kingdoms at once*

**Text:** 1 John 2:3-29 · **Supporting:** John 13:34 · Leviticus 19:18 · Matthew 6:24 · 1 Corinthians 7:31

There is a kind of Christianity that asks how it knows it is saved and answers by looking inward, at a feeling, a memory, a date on a card from a summer camp. John has watched teachers leave who were sure of themselves, who never doubted their own spirituality for a moment, and he refuses to ground assurance in a feeling. He grounds it in two things you can watch yourself do or fail to do. Obedience and love. "And hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments" (1 John 2:3). Not if we feel him. If we keep him.

**Knowing, Measured by Keeping**

John does not flinch from the implication. "He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him" (1 John 2:4). This is the second test of the letter, and it lands hard on anyone who has divided their religion into belief and behavior, treating the first as essential and the second as advanced. John will not let the seam hold. The knowledge of God is not a deposit in the head that may or may not reach the hands. "But whoso keepeth his word, in him verily is the love of God perfected" (1 John 2:5). The keeping is the evidence the knowing was real.

Then he does something curious. He calls his commandment both old and new. "Brethren, I write no new commandment unto you, but an old commandment which ye had from the beginning... Again, a new commandment I write unto you" (1 John 2:7-8). Old, because love of neighbor stood in the law: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (Leviticus 19:18). New, because Jesus gave it a measure the law never had. "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you" (John 13:34). The standard moved. Love your neighbor as yourself was the floor. Love as I have loved you, to the cross, is the height. The same commandment, raised.

And here John presses the test against the dark. "He that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now" (1 John 2:9). You may have walked away from a brother and called it discernment. You may have written someone off and called it wisdom. John gives it one name. Darkness.

**The Heart That Cannot Hold Two Loves**

Then he names the rival. "Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him" (1 John 2:15). This is not a command to despise creation, or to feel guilty for a good meal. The world here is the system organized against God, the order running on three engines John names exactly: "the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life" (1 John 2:16). The appetite that must be fed. The eye that must acquire. The self that must be seen as someone. That is the world's liturgy, and it is teaching you to want what it wants.

Jesus had already said it could not be split. "No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon" (Matthew 6:24). Not should not. Cannot. The heart is not large enough to hold the Father and the world at full devotion, because each is asking for the same room, the center. And here is the mercy hidden in the warning: the thing John tells you not to love is leaving anyway. "And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever" (1 John 2:17). Paul said the same to Corinth, "the fashion of this world passeth away" (1 Corinthians 7:31). You are being asked to loosen your grip on something that is already sliding off the table.

I know the pull, because I have felt the love of the Father go thin in me precisely when the love of the world ran high, and I did not notice it as idolatry. It never feels like idolatry while you are doing it. It feels like ambition, like provision, like simply wanting a good life. The competition for the center is quiet. You do not feel the Father being edged out. You only notice, one ordinary morning, that he is not at the center anymore, and you cannot remember the day he moved.

**The Anointing That Keeps You Abiding**

So how does anyone love the Father in a world built to capture the heart? Not by willpower. John points to a gift. "But ye have an unction from the Holy One, and ye know all things" (1 John 2:20). The anointing, the Spirit given to ordinary believers, is what keeps them in the truth when the teachers who departed insisted the truth was an elite secret. "These things have I written unto you concerning them that seduce you. But the anointing which ye have received of him abideth in you" (1 John 2:26-27).

And the whole thing rests, as it always does in John, on Christ. The love we owe a brother is the love Christ first laid down. The commandment we cannot keep on our own is kept in those who abide in the one who kept it perfectly. "And now, little children, abide in him; that, when he shall appear, we may have confidence, and not be ashamed before him at his coming" (1 John 2:28). The test is not finally a measure of how strong your love is. It is a measure of whether you are abiding in the One whose love does not pass away with the world.

Love the Father, not the world.

## Children of God, and Love That Costs Something
*The Father's name on people who do not yet look like it*

**Text:** 1 John 3:1-24 · **Supporting:** John 13:35 · Genesis 4:8 · James 2:15-16 · Romans 8:16-17

There is a love that costs nothing and a love that costs everything, and most of us have spent our lives confusing the two. The first announces itself, it speaks, it posts, it sends the message at the right moment, it feels warm and asks for nothing. The second shows up at a hospital, opens a wallet, gives up an evening, dies a little. John has watched a church learn to say love and not do it, and in chapter three he refuses to let the word float free of the deed any longer.

**A Name We Do Not Yet Look Like**

He begins not with the cost but with the gift, and the gift is staggering. "Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God" (1 John 3:1). Behold, stop and look at this, because it is not ordinary. The God who is light has put his own name on us. And then John names the strange experience of carrying that name in a world that does not see it: "therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not." You wear the Father's name and the room does not recognize it, because the room never recognized him either.

Then the honest tension. "Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is" (1 John 3:2). Now and not yet, held in one sentence. The status is settled, now are we the sons of God. The appearance is unfinished, it doth not yet appear what we shall be. Paul says the same: the Spirit "beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God" (Romans 8:16). The verdict is in. The resemblance is still being worked. And John says that very hope does something while you wait: "And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure" (1 John 3:3). Hope is not passive. The man who knows he will be like Christ starts becoming like him now.

**Cain at the Altar**

Then John reaches all the way back for his example of love's opposite, and he does not pick a murderer in the headlines. He picks a worshiper. "Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. And wherefore slew he him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's righteous" (1 John 3:12). Look at where Cain was when the hatred took hold. At the altar. Bringing an offering. Genesis tells it plainly: "Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him" (Genesis 4:8). The first murder in Scripture is committed by a man who had just been at worship, against a brother whose only offense was being accepted.

John's point is a knife. "Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer" (1 John 3:15). He has moved the line. You thought hatred and murder were separated by a great distance, the distance between feeling something and doing it. John says they are the same root, and Cain proves it: the hatred was complete in the heart at the altar; the field only let it finish. "Marvel not, my brethren, if the world hate you" (1 John 3:13). The world has been Cain to Abel since the beginning, and it does not need a reason beyond your righteousness.

I have stood at the altar with Cain's heart. I have led worship while resenting a brother whose acceptance exposed my works as evil, and I called my resentment a difference of vision. The respectable do not slay in the field. We slay in the silence, the dropped friendship, the withheld good word, the brother written out of the story. Whosoever hateth his brother. John leaves no room to stand outside that.

**Love in Deed, Because He Laid Down His Life**

So what is the love that proves we have passed from death to life? John defines it by a single act and a single person. "Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren" (1 John 3:16). There it is, the new measure from chapter two, now made concrete. Love is not a sentiment Christ felt toward us. It is a life Christ laid down for us. And the imitation John asks for is not heroic martyrdom in the abstract; he immediately makes it ordinary and expensive: "But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?" (1 John 3:17).

James put the same scene in front of his church, a brother naked and hungry, and a believer who says, "Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled," and gives them nothing (James 2:15-16). John's verdict on that empty word is the heart of the chapter: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth" (1 John 3:18). The world will know us, Jesus said, "if ye have love one to another" (John 13:35). Not if we say it. If we lay it down.

And notice where John lands, not on our performance but on the costly love that came first. We can love in deed only because Christ first laid down his life in deed. The inheritance Paul names is bought at that price: we are "heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him" (Romans 8:17). The children of God are known by a love that costs something, because the Father who named them paid everything to do it.

Love in deed and truth.

## Test the Spirits, Because God Is Love
*The love you cannot fake and the confession you cannot skip*

**Text:** 1 John 4:1-21 · **Supporting:** John 3:16 · Romans 5:8 · 1 Corinthians 12:3 · 1 John 4:20

We live with a strange superstition that spiritual experience certifies itself, that if something feels transcendent, moving, full of energy and conviction, it must be from God. John has buried more than one church under that superstition. The teachers who left were not cold; they were inspired. They claimed a spirit. And so John opens chapter four with a sentence that refuses to let sincerity stand in for truth. "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world" (1 John 4:1).

**The Test the Whole Letter Hangs On**

The test is not the intensity of the experience. It is the content of the confession. "Hereby know ye the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God: and every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God" (1 John 4:2-3). Come in the flesh. The teachers who departed would say Jesus, would say Christ, would speak warmly of the spiritual Redeemer, but they would not nail him to a body, to history, to a cross that bled. Paul drew the same line for Corinth: "no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost" (1 Corinthians 12:3). The confession is not a password. It is the dividing line, because a Christ without flesh is a Christ who never died for sin, and a Christ who never died for sin cannot save anyone.

This is the third test of the letter, alongside walking in the light and loving the brethren, and John has now laid all three on the table. What you believe about Christ. How you treat your brother. Whether you walk in the light. The teachers had spirit and intensity and felt no need of any of the three. John says try the spirits, and the test is whether they will confess the Christ who came in flesh and stayed in it all the way to the tree.

**God Is Love, and Love Has a Definition**

Then John makes the great statement, and it is the most quoted and most abused line in the letter. "He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love" (1 John 4:8). The world has taken those three words and made them a permission slip, God is love, therefore God affirms whatever I love, whatever I want, whatever feels like love to me. But John will not let the phrase float. He defines it in the next breath, and he defines it by an act, not a feeling. "In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (1 John 4:9-10).

There is the word again, propitiation. The same word from chapter two. God is love, and the proof of it is not a sunset or a feeling but a Son sent to absorb the wrath our sin had earned. Paul says it with the same scandal: "God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). And John's earlier teacher had said it first: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son" (John 3:16). Loved, gave. Love in John is never the thing we generated and offered up. It is the thing we received while we were enemies. "Herein is love, not that we loved God." Strike that out and the whole gospel inverts into a religion of our sincerity. Keep it, and love becomes a gift before it is ever a command.

**The Brother You Have Seen**

And here John closes the trap, gently and completely. "We love him, because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19). The order is the entire Christian life in five words. Not we love and therefore he loves. He first loved, and therefore we can. The love we are commanded to give is not manufactured from our own reserves; it is the overflow of a love poured in first. "Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another" (1 John 4:11). If. So. Then. The whole obligation rests on the gift.

Then the verse that ends every escape. "If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" (1 John 4:20). John knows the religious heart. He knows we would rather love God than love the brother across the table, because God does not interrupt us, does not disappoint us, does not need the wallet opened or the evening given. The invisible God is easier to love than the visible brother. And John says that is exactly the lie. The brother you can see is the test of the God you cannot.

I have claimed to love God on a Sunday while carrying contempt for a brother I would see on Monday, and I have felt no contradiction in it at all. That is how deep the lie runs, it does not even register as a lie. John drags it into the light: he is a liar. Not mistaken. A liar. The love of God that does not reach the brother is a love I invented, and an invented love proves nothing about the God who is love.

We cannot fake the love that came from him, because we never had it until he gave it. "And this commandment have we from him, That he who loveth God love his brother also" (1 John 4:21).

We love because he first loved.

## The Faith That Overcomes, and the Knowledge of Eternal Life
*Assurance is not a mood. It is a testimony.*

**Text:** 1 John 5:1-21 · **Supporting:** John 16:33 · John 5:24 · Romans 8:38-39 · 1 John 5:13

John has spent four chapters handing people tests, and a certain kind of believer reaches the end of those tests more anxious than when they began. Do I really walk in the light? Do I love my brother enough? Is my confession of Christ pure enough? If the letter ended at chapter four, it would leave the tender conscience trembling and the proud conscience smug, exactly the two it meant to correct. So John writes a fifth chapter, and its whole purpose is not to lower the tests but to ground the assurance under them in something outside the self. Not in your feelings. In God's testimony.

**The Faith That Overcomes the World**

He begins by tying belief and love together one last time. "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God: and every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him" (1 John 5:1). The new birth is the root; faith and love are the fruit. You do not believe and love your way into being born of God. You are born of God, and then you believe and love. And then the great word of the chapter: "For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith" (1 John 5:4).

Overcometh. The world that John told you not to love in chapter two, the world that is passing away, the world that hated Cain's brother and hates you, that world is already a defeated thing for the one born of God. Not because the believer is strong. Because the believer's faith is fastened to the One who has already won. Jesus said it the night before he died: "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). The victory is his. Faith is simply the hand that holds onto the Victor. "Who is he that overcometh the world, but he that believeth that Jesus is the Son of God?" (1 John 5:5).

**The Testimony God Has Given**

Then John moves from the believer's faith to God's witness, and this is the hinge of the chapter. He is not content to leave assurance resting on the quality of our believing, because the quality of our believing rises and falls with our sleep and our circumstances. So he points to a testimony that does not move. "If we receive the witness of men, the witness of God is greater: for this is the witness of God which he hath testified of his Son" (1 John 5:9). We trust the word of men a hundred times a day, the doctor, the pilot, the headline. God has given his own sworn word about his Son, and it is greater than any of them, and to disbelieve it is to call God a liar: "he that believeth not God hath made him a liar; because he believeth not the record that God gave of his Son" (1 John 5:10).

And here is the record, the heart of the whole letter's comfort: "And this is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life" (1 John 5:11-12). Eternal life is not a wage you earn by passing the tests. It is a gift God has already given, and it is located in a person. The life is in his Son. The question of assurance, then, is not finally How am I doing? It is Do I have the Son? And if you have the Son, you have the life, because the life is in him and nowhere else.

**That You May Know**

John states his purpose plainly, and it is the opposite of anxiety. "These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life" (1 John 5:13). Know. Not hope. Not wish. Not work yourself toward a trembling maybe. The whole letter, with all its hard tests, was written so that the people of God would know. Jesus had promised the same certainty: "He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life" (John 5:24). Hath. Is passed. Present tense, settled, done. Paul reaches the same ground at the end of Romans 8 and dares the universe to break it: "neither death, nor life... shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:38-39).

I have spent nights measuring my assurance by my own performance and found it thin every time, because a man who looks inward for certainty will always find a reason to doubt, and a proud man will always find a reason not to. That is why John drives us out of ourselves and onto the testimony. The advocate who pleaded my case in chapter one and the propitiation who bore my wrath in chapters two and four is the same Son in whom this eternal life is kept. My assurance is not the warmth of my feeling about Christ. It is the coldness of a fact about Christ: God has given eternal life, and it is in his Son, and I have the Son.

So John ends not with a feeling but with a stack of certainties: "We know that whosoever is born of God sinneth not... And we know that we are of God... And we know that the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true" (1 John 5:18-20). Three times, we know, we know, we know. The man who began by handling the Word of Life with his hands ends by putting certainty into the hands of trembling people. "This is the true God, and eternal life." The life he touched is the life he gives, and the One who is the propitiation for our sins is himself the eternal life we possess.

Know that you have life.
